title: Agents and Guardrails
summary: After this intermediate module, learners can map an agent loop, place guardrails at its decision and action boundaries, and design tests that verify both permitted and denied behavior. Learners can also distinguish a behavioral policy from the mechanisms that enforce it.
objectives: Identify the observations, decisions, actions, and feedback that form an agent loop.
Distinguish a behavioral policy from an enforcement mechanism.
Place preventive, runtime, and post-action guardrails at appropriate boundaries.
Design tests covering permitted actions, denied actions, ambiguous requests, and attempted bypasses.
Explain why controls at an action boundary are needed even when outputs are checked.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previously cited source was content/modules/ai-foundations/agents-and-guardrails.json. That internal path had an unregistered publisher, had never been verified, and was not a directly resolvable HTTPS source.

This update replaces that citation with canonical arXiv records for the ReAct, Constitutional AI, and ToolEmu papers. The change affects source provenance, the support for the agent-loop and guardrail material, and the module's verification metadata. It does not introduce a provider-specific implementation, product configuration, or version-dependent instruction.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that a learner understands the basic idea of a model receiving input and producing output. It does not assume experience with a particular provider, programming library, agent framework, or security product.

The module uses tool as a generic term for an external capability an agent can request, such as retrieving a record or submitting a change. It focuses on reasoning about control boundaries rather than configuring a named implementation.

sections.title: Map the agent loop
paragraphs: A useful agent-loop model has four stages: observe the current state, decide what to do next, request an action, and inspect the resulting observation before continuing or stopping. The ReAct paper describes an approach that interleaves reasoning traces with actions and incorporates observations from those actions.

This loop differs from treating a model response as the final result. An agent can use an observation from one action to select a later action. That repeated interaction creates additional control boundaries because an action can affect an external system before the agent produces its final response.

To map a workflow, write down the information the agent can observe, the actions it may request, the conditions under which each action is allowed, the result returned after an action, and the conditions that end or escalate the loop.
sections.callout: A model's proposed action is not the same as an authorized action. Treat proposal and execution as separate steps.

sections.title: Separate policy from enforcement
paragraphs: A policy states the intended behavior, including what actions are permitted, prohibited, or require review. An enforcement mechanism checks or limits behavior at a specific boundary. Keeping these concepts separate makes it possible to test whether an implementation actually enforces its stated policy.

The Constitutional AI paper describes the use of written principles to guide critique and revision. For an agent workflow, written principles can help express expected behavior, but a statement of principles alone does not authorize or block an external action.

For example, a policy might say that an agent may read a calendar but must not modify it without approval. An enforcement mechanism would check the requested operation and approval state before allowing a calendar-writing action to execute.

sections.title: Place guardrails at control boundaries
paragraphs: Before the loop begins, input checks can reject an unsupported request or route an ambiguous request for clarification. At the decision boundary, the system can restrict the set of actions available for the current task. At the action boundary, it can validate the proposed action, its arguments, and the required authorization before execution.

During the loop, runtime checks can stop repeated failures, unexpected action sequences, or requests outside the declared task. After an action, the returned observation can be checked before it is used in another decision. Before a final response is delivered, an output check can detect content that should be withheld or escalated.

The ToolEmu paper studies risks arising when language-model agents interact with tools and evaluates risky behavior in an emulated environment. Its focus on action-related risk supports testing the interaction loop rather than evaluating only the final text.

A final-output check cannot reverse an external action that has already occurred. When an action can change external state, the allow-or-deny decision belongs before execution. Post-action checks remain useful for detecting problems, stopping further steps, recording the event, and escalating review.

sections.title: Test permitted and denied behavior
paragraphs: Begin with a policy statement and turn each rule into observable test cases. Include a permitted case that should complete, a prohibited case that should be denied, a case missing required information that should request clarification, and a case requiring review that should pause before execution.

Test the boundary where enforcement occurs. For an action requiring approval, verify that the action is not executed without approval, that valid approval permits only the intended action, and that changing the action after approval causes another check.

Include attempted bypasses, such as placing conflicting instructions inside retrieved content or asking for the same prohibited effect through a different action sequence. The expected result should identify whether the request is denied, clarified, or escalated. A test is incomplete when it records only the final wording and does not determine whether an external action occurred.

Record the initial request, relevant observations, proposed actions, authorization decisions, executed actions, returned results, stop reason, and test outcome. These records let a reviewer locate the boundary at which expected and observed behavior diverged.

sections.title: Apply the method
paragraphs: First, draw the agent loop and list every point where information enters, an action is proposed, an action is executed, or a result returns. Second, state the policy for each action in plain language. Third, assign an enforcement mechanism to the boundary that can prevent the disallowed effect.

Fourth, define what should happen when a check fails: deny the action, request clarification, stop the loop, or escalate for review. Fifth, create paired tests for allowed and disallowed behavior. Finally, inspect both the final response and the action record.

After completing this process, a learner can move from a general instruction such as act safely to a reviewable control plan that specifies what is checked, where it is checked, and how correct enforcement is demonstrated.

questions.prompt: What feature of the workflow makes the agent loop different from treating one model response as the final result?
choices: It can use an observation from one action to select a later action.
It always executes every available action.
It removes the need for an explicit stopping condition.
It guarantees that proposed actions are authorized.
questions.explanation: The module defines the loop as observing, deciding, requesting an action, and using the resulting observation before continuing or stopping.

questions.prompt: Which option is an enforcement mechanism rather than a policy statement?
choices: The agent should avoid unauthorized changes.
Calendar changes require approval.
A check blocks a calendar-writing action when approval is absent.
The agent should behave safely.
questions.explanation: A policy states intended behavior. The check is an enforcement mechanism because it evaluates the approval state and blocks execution at the action boundary.

questions.prompt: Where should a guardrail decide whether to allow an action that can change external state?
choices: Only after the final response is delivered.
Before the action is executed.
Only after the changed state is observed.
After every action in the loop has finished.
questions.explanation: The module explains that a final-output check cannot reverse an external action that has already occurred, so the allow-or-deny decision belongs before execution.

questions.prompt: Which test best verifies a rule that an action requires approval?
choices: Confirm that the final response sounds cautious.
Confirm that the action executes both with and without approval.
Confirm that the action is blocked without approval and permitted with valid approval for the intended action.
Confirm only that the agent can describe the approval rule.
questions.explanation: The test must observe enforcement at the action boundary, including denial without approval and permission only when approval matches the intended action.

questions.prompt: What did the citation update affect?
choices: It added instructions for a named provider.
It changed source provenance, support for the material, and verification metadata.
It introduced a product configuration key.
It converted the module to an advanced level.
questions.explanation: The update section states that the unverified internal citation was replaced with canonical arXiv records, affecting provenance, support, and verification metadata.
